extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in natural language processing / computational narrative (automatic story generation)
extracted.subtask_description: A survey of challenges and attempted approaches in automatic story generation, focusing on controllability, commonsense integration, character/entity modeling, creativity, and evaluation. Intended as a starting point for researchers entering computational narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controllability (user influence over generation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The controllability problem in story generation is the user input’s ability to influence the generation results (e.g., making the system adhere to a desired plot or ending).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches include reinforcement learning, model fusion, plan-and-write, generation-by-interpolation, and outline-conditioned transformers. Controllability is a major challenge introduced/complicated by neural models which tend to produce unstructured outputs; trade-offs include decreased creativity/interestingness and remaining issues with coherence and logical plot generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controllability Goal Type: ending-focused vs storyline-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Two primary controllability goals: generate a specific ending (ending-focused) or generate according to an outline/plotline (storyline-focused).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ending-focused systems (e.g., Tambwekar et al., Wang et al.) aim to reach a target ending; storyline-focused systems (e.g., Rashkin et al., Yao et al., Fan et al.) condition on outlines or premises. Which goal a system targets affects evaluation and design (e.g., reward shaping for endings vs plan-based control for storylines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal achievement (distance-to-goal & story-verb-frequency reward components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of success for ending-guided control such as distance to the goal verb and story verb frequency used in reward shaping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tambwekar et al. define reward as (1) distance to goal verb: how many lines between a generated verb and the goal verb in training stories, and (2) story verb frequency: counts of stories with both the goal verb and generated verb. These helped in plot coherence and goal achievement but may require retraining per goal (usability drawback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot coherence / logical ordering / narrative flow
rubrics_metrics.description: The generated story should exhibit logical ordering of events, coherent narrative flow, and internally consistent plot progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluated by human preference studies and automatic coherence rankers (e.g., RoBERTa-based coherence scoring). Techniques that help include explicit storyline outlines, memory/state tracking, discourse representations, and coherence-ranking of candidate storylines. Despite improvements, logical inconsistencies remain a major open problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (inter-story and intra-story repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of undesired repetition both within a story (intra-story) and across generated stories (inter-story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yao et al. proposed inter-story and intra-story repetition metrics. Repetition is a common failure mode of neural generators; models (e.g., transformer-based) reduce some repetition but it's still a key evaluation axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perplexity (language-model likelihood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perplexity is used as a standard automatic metric indicating how well a model predicts text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perplexity is commonly reported (and was used in some controllability evaluations) but is a weak proxy for story quality (doesn't capture coherence, creativity, or narrative structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: BLEU / ROUGE (n-gram overlap metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard n-gram overlap metrics used in other NLG tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics are used in story generation work but are insufficient for story-specific qualities (creativity, interestingness, event/character organization). The paper emphasizes the need for story-specific metrics beyond BLEU/ROUGE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity and interestingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-judged qualities like novelty, figurative language, compelling characters, and intriguing plots that make a story engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controlled models often suffer from low creativity, especially when constrained by rigid outlines. The field lacks good automatic measures for creativity/interestingness; developing such metrics is highlighted as a priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonsense knowledge (acquisition and incorporation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared real-world knowledge about how the world works is necessary for coherent, plausible narratives; challenges include how to acquire such knowledge and integrate it into story generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common approaches include fine-tuning on commonsense datasets, using models that generate or rank commonsense inferences, and incorporating knowledge graphs into encoders. Bottlenecks remain in obtaining paragraph- and story-level commonsense inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonsense benchmark: ConceptNet
rubrics_metrics.description: ConceptNet is a large semantic knowledge graph connecting words/phrases with labeled edges representing general human knowledge (e.g., (dog, HasA, tail)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widely used as a source for training or augmenting models; can be transformed into natural sentences for further training. Serves as a foundational external knowledge resource.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonsense benchmark: CommonsenseQA
rubrics_metrics.description: A benchmark extracting from ConceptNet providing multiple-choice questions that require commonsense disambiguation; state-of-the-art LMs obtain only modest accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to gauge commonsense capabilities of models; highlights the gap between large pre-trained LMs and human-level commonsense reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonsense benchmark: ATOMIC
rubrics_metrics.description: ATOMIC is a dataset of ~877K textual descriptions of If-then relations focusing on event sequences and social commonsense (organized into categories like xIntent, xEffect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for training models to predict social and event-related commonsense inferences relevant to narrative events and character actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonsense benchmark: GLUCOSE
rubrics_metrics.description: GLUCOSE is a large-scale dataset of implicit commonsense causal knowledge with story-specific causal statements generalized into inference rules across ten dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to capture causal explanations relevant to story sentences and events; complements ATOMIC's person-centric inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonsense benchmark: SocialIQA and other QA-style datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: SocialIQA and other datasets (MC-Script, OpenBookQA, Cosmos QA) provide multiple-choice or QA-style tasks focused on social reasoning, script knowledge, and contextual commonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These datasets provide varied evaluation targets for commonsense reasoning components of story generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frameworks for integrating commonsense: fine-tuning, perception-analysis, encoding incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Three ways to apply commonsense resources: (1) fine-tune pre-trained LMs on commonsense benchmarks, (2) analyze/derive perceptions of causality after generation, (3) incorporate knowledge graphs into model encodings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each approach has trade-offs: fine-tuning improves local logicality/grammaticality but not necessarily long-range coherence; inference-based methods (COMeT/PARA-COMeT) can generate inferences but may be sentence-level; graph-encoding improves end-prediction and reasoning in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level vs paragraph-level vs story-level commonsense inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Levels at which commonsense inference operates: many models perform sentence-level inference (e.g., COMeT), some work on paragraph-level (PARA-COMeT), but story-level inference remains an open need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentence-level inference is limited (e.g., token-length constraints); paragraph- and story-level inferences are desirable to capture episodic and global causal relations necessary for plausible long narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory/state tracking and discourse representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit maintenance of memory state vectors and discourse-type encodings (e.g., introduction/body/conclusion) to track narrative state across generation steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PlotMachines uses memory and discourse encodings appended to outlines to improve logical ordering and narrative flow. Such mechanisms help with long-term dependency and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline representation quality (granularity & completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: How outlines are represented (unordered high-level multi-word event descriptions, ordered event lists, titles, etc.) and how comprehensive they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple outlines help control generation but may produce shallow stories; richer event-based planning outputs can improve depth and interestingness. The representation choice affects extractability and controllability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt quality and prompt specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of the writing prompts or premises conditioning generation (auto-generated prompts vs human-written prompts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auto-generated prompts tend to be generic and less interesting than human prompts, often leading to boring stories. Conditioning on better premises/titles can improve plot consistency and interest without retraining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entity representation and coreference consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Dynamic, up-to-date entity vectors or entity-anonymization pipelines to represent characters and entities and maintain mention/coreference consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models like ENGEN and EntityNLM update entity representations on mentions and can improve fluency and mention generation tasks; pipelines that anonymize entities during planning and de-anonymize later can improve generalization. Effect on long-term plot advancement is still unclear and requires further evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character modeling: emotion arcs and character affinities
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling character affect (emotion arcs) and inter-character affinities to inform narrative progression and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches include conditioning generation on an emotion arc (EC-EM, EC-CLF rewards) or modeling affinities with discrete categories (foe/indifferent/friend/mate). Emotion-consistency rewards (classifier probability or Levenshtein-like distance over inferred reactions) improved emotion faithfulness but often focus on a single protagonist rather than multi-character dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation via human preference studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Using human raters (e.g., Mechanical Turk) to compare continuations or full stories on fluency, coherence, and preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human evaluations remain a central component for assessing narrative quality; automatic metrics correlate imperfectly with human judgments so preference tests are frequently used to compare models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb diversity / action-driven narrative quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures and modeling choices to increase verb/action diversity and produce action-driven narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRL + entity pipelines and attention heads dedicated to past verbs can increase verb diversity and improve perceived coherence for action-driven story generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model practicality and usability (retraining and user convenience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical constraints such as whether a control method requires retraining for each new goal or user-specified control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some RL-based control methods require per-goal retraining, which reduces user convenience. Methods that condition on generated premises or outlines without retraining are preferable for usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for unified, story-specific evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The field lacks robust, unified metrics tailored to stories (capturing creativity, interestingness, event/character organization) to enable fair comparisons across systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current reliance on BLEU, ROUGE, and perplexity is inadequate. The paper highlights development of measures for creativity, interestingness, organization of events and characters, and story-level coherence as a key future direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-range coherence and entity/event consistency across multi-paragraph stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining consistent events, entities, and causal relations over paragraphs and entire stories (not only sentence-level coherence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformer-based models improved but still struggle with commonsense inference and long-range consistency; integration of external human knowledge and memory mechanisms is suggested to address this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction and generalization (SRL + entity / action-plans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using abstractions (action plans, predicate-argument sequences, anonymized entities) to learn generalizable story rules and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstraction pipelines (SRL + entity) enable models to learn verb-argument patterns and generalize across contexts, improving coherence and verb diversity; but their effect on multi-agent interactions and full-plot development needs more study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of current commonsense inference models (performance ceiling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many commonsense-inference-based methods improve local causality/perceptions but are constrained by the inference models' quality and sentence-length limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CCPO and PARA-COMeT show gains in local/global coherence, but overall performance is restricted by the underlying commonsense inference capacity; advancing inference models is necessary for better story-level reasoning.
